body.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Four people must cross a rickety bridge at night. The bridge holds at most two people at once, there is only one torch, and nobody may cross without it. The four walk at different speeds: alone, they need 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes to cross. When two cross together, they move at the slower person's pace. Everyone must be across within 17 minutes. It sounds impossible - the two slowest alone seem to eat the whole budget.

The obvious plan fails: have the fastest walker escort everyone. That costs 10 (escorting the slowest), 1 (returning), 5, 1 and 2 - a total of 19 minutes. Two minutes too many. The fix requires questioning the assumption that the fastest person should do all the escorting.

body.heading: The seventeen-minute solution
paragraphs: Send the 1-minute and 2-minute walkers across together: 2 minutes. The 1-minute walker returns with the torch: 1 minute, total 3. Now the trick - send the 5-minute and 10-minute walkers across together: 10 minutes, total 13. The 2-minute walker, waiting on the far side, brings the torch back: 2 minutes, total 15. Finally the 1 and 2 cross together: 2 minutes, total 17 exactly.

The saving came from pairing the two slowest walkers. When the 5-minute walker crosses with the fastest escort, her 5 minutes are paid in full; when she crosses with the 10-minute walker, her time hides completely inside his. Whenever a problem charges you for the maximum of a pair, ask whether two expensive items can be overlapped.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Change the times to 1, 3, 6 and 9 minutes and find the best plan. (Hint: the slow-pair trick gives 3 + 1 + 9 + 3 + 3 = 19 minutes, beating the escort-everyone plan of 20.) Then try 1, 2, 4 and 8 and see whether the same shape of solution still wins.

For the real connoisseur version, ask what happens with five walkers, or when the bridge holds three. The puzzle generalises beautifully, and the slow-pair idea remains the key that unlocks most versions.

takeaway: Send the two slowest across together: pairing them hides the second-slowest time inside the slowest, which is where the saving lives.
